title: Flexing what is delivered; burn charts at every level
blurb: Explain how PRINCE2 Agile tracks progress by what is delivered, why time and cost are not the focus, and where burn charts fit at team, stage and project level.
question: In a PRINCE2 Agile project, why is a burn chart a natural way to show progress at every level of the project?

teach.h: What the progress practice is for
teach.body: The progress practice sets up ways to monitor and compare what has actually been achieved against what was planned, to forecast whether the project's objectives and continued viability are still on track, and to control any deviation that would cause an exception. In plain English: where are we, where will we end up, and do we need to escalate? That purpose is unchanged in PRINCE2 Agile; what changes is what you watch most closely.

teach.h: The progress practice in four moves

steps.label: Control
steps.sub: Act on deviations causing an exception

teach.caption: Purpose of the progress practice (12.1). Control mixes time-based and event-based controls (5.3.1.7).

teach.h: Flex what is delivered, not time or cost
teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile sets zero tolerance for extra time and extra cost on all levels of plan. Scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves. So the aspect of performance that interests the whole project management team most is flexibility in what is delivered. Tracking spend against a budget tolerance, or time against a time tolerance, tells you little when both tolerances are zero.

Because flex in what is delivered is the focus, showing it as a burn chart is natural whatever the level. At team level a burn-down usually plots story points remaining over the days of an iteration. At release, stage and project level a burn-up usually plots completed work over iterations or stages against the total scope, to forecast when the work will be finished. The same idea, done versus still to do, runs from the team to the board.

levels.label: Stage or release: burn-up over iterations

teach.h: Release burn-up: will the Musts land?
teach.caption: About 20 points per iteration: the Musts are safe, some Coulds will not fit. Flex scope, not the date.

teach.h: How agile teams monitor and report
teach.body: One way to monitor is to set baseline metrics through assessments and then check the same metrics regularly; delivery teams use flow metrics such as Kanban lead time. Reporting is still taken seriously, but it is often informal, through workshops such as planning, review and retrospectives, and visual, through burn charts and dashboards. Feedback loops are short and frequent. The project manager may attend the team's daily stand-up only with the delivery team's agreement.

Northmoor is building a tenant repairs portal with two delivery teams. Project manager Priya Nair stops sending the board a spend-versus-budget table: each iteration has a fixed team and fixed length, so cost and time cannot drift. Instead she shows a release burn-up with the Must-have line marked. After iteration 3 it shows every Must landing, but two Could-have stories will not fit, so product owner Tom Okafor moves them to a later release. The date and budget stay put.

teach.text: Do not track progress mainly as spend against budget or time against tolerance: in PRINCE2 Agile both have zero tolerance, so the flex, and the thing to watch, is what is delivered. Also keep the purposes apart: controlling deviations that cause an exception is PROGRESS; controlling changes to the baseline is ISSUES.

items: Progress practice: monitor and compare actual against planned, forecast, control deviations causing an exception (12.1).
Time and cost have zero tolerance on all levels of plan; what is delivered flexes.
Flex in what is delivered is the primary aspect of interest, so burn charts suit every level (12.3.1).
Team level: burn-down over days; project or product level: burn-up over iterations or stages.
Monitoring uses baseline metrics such as lead time; reporting is informal and visual (12.2).
The PM may attend daily stand-ups with the delivery team's agreement.

summary: You can now explain why PRINCE2 Agile watches what is delivered rather than time and cost, and how burn charts show it at team, stage and project level. You can also describe how agile teams monitor and report progress informally and visually.

A.q: Which is a purpose of the progress practice?
options: To control changes to the project's baseline
To control deviations that cause an exception
To identify and assess uncertainties
To define the structure of accountability
A.why: The progress practice monitors and compares actual against planned, forecasts, and controls any deviations causing an exception (12.1).

whyNot.0: Controlling changes to the baseline is the purpose of the issues practice.
whyNot.2: Identifying and assessing uncertainties is the purpose of the risk practice.
whyNot.3: Defining accountability and responsibilities is the purpose of the organization practice.

A.q: Which performance aspect does PRINCE2 Agile see as of most interest to the whole project management team when tracking progress?
options: Spend against the budget
Time against the end date
Flexibility in what is delivered
Risk exposure across iterations
A.why: Flexibility in what is delivered is probably the primary aspect of interest, which is why burn charts suit every level (12.3.1).

whyNot.0: Cost has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, so tracking spend against budget adds little.
whyNot.1: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, so it is not where the flex sits.
whyNot.3: Risk exposure across iterations is shown by a cumulative risk burn-down in the risk practice.

A.q: What are the PRINCE2 Agile default tolerances for time and cost?
options: Zero tolerance for extra time and extra cost on all levels of plan
Time flexed for Could haves; cost fixed at the project level
Small tolerances set by the team for each iteration
Tolerances agreed for the stage plan but not for teams
A.why: Table 3.1: zero tolerance for extra time and zero tolerance for extra cost on all levels of plan.

whyNot.1: Could haves flex scope, not time; time is fixed on all levels of plan.
whyNot.2: Teams do not set their own time or cost tolerances; the default is zero.
whyNot.3: The zero tolerance applies on all levels of plan, including team level.

B.q: At which level does PRINCE2 Agile consider a burn chart a natural way to show progress?
options: Team level, within an iteration
Project level, across stages
Stage level, across releases
Any level of the project
B.why: Because flex in what is delivered matters at every level, displaying it as a burn chart is natural irrespective of the project level (12.3.1).

whyNot.0: Teams do use burn-downs, but burn charts are not limited to the team level.
whyNot.1: Burn-ups are common at project level, but burn charts suit every level.
whyNot.2: Stage-level burn charts are useful, but the guidance covers all levels.

B.q:
Which two statements about monitoring and reporting progress in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. Baseline metrics can be set through assessments and checked regularly.
2. Reporting is often handled informally through workshops and visually.
3. Detailed written reports replace workshops for agile teams.
4. The project manager attends every daily stand-up by default.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
B.why: 12.2: progress can be monitored with baseline metrics checked regularly (1), and reporting is often informal through workshops and visual via burn charts and dashboards (2).

whyNot.1: Statement 4 is wrong: the PM may attend daily stand-ups with the delivery team's agreement.
whyNot.2: Statement 3 is wrong: reporting is often informal and visual, through workshops.
whyNot.3: Both are wrong: reporting is informal and visual, and the PM attends stand-ups with the team's agreement.

B.q: A release burn-up shows that every Must have will be delivered but some Could haves will not fit before the release date. What is the PRINCE2 Agile response?
options: Move the release date to fit the Could haves
Raise an exception report to the board
Leave the Could haves for a later release
Add a temporary team to finish them all
B.why: Scope is fixed for Musts and flexed for Shoulds and Coulds, while time and cost have zero tolerance, so the Coulds are the flex (Table 3.1).

whyNot.0: Time has zero tolerance; moving the release date breaks it.
whyNot.1: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded: dropping Coulds is within the agreed flex.
whyNot.3: Adding a team adds cost, which also has zero tolerance.

C.q: Why is tracking spend against a budget tolerance of little value in a PRINCE2 Agile project, and what is tracked instead?
options: Cost is the project executive's concern; teams track velocity
Cost has zero tolerance; progress tracks what is delivered
Budgets are agreed per release; progress tracks the risk register
Cost flexes with scope; progress tracks hours worked by teams
C.why: With zero tolerance on cost on all levels of plan there is no point tracking spend against tolerance; the flex is in what is delivered, shown by burn charts (12.3.1, Table 3.1).

whyNot.0: Cost matters to the board, but the reason is its zero tolerance, and velocity is one input to burn charts rather than the thing tracked.
whyNot.2: The risk register records risks; it is not the measure of delivery progress.
whyNot.3: Cost does not flex in PRINCE2 Agile, and burn charts plot story points, not hours.

C.q: A team's iteration burn-down and the project's burn-up are both shown to stakeholders. Which pairing of chart and usual level is correct?
options: Burn-down at project level over stages; burn-up at team level over days
Burn-down and burn-up both at team level over days
Burn-down at board level; burn-up at work package level
Burn-down at team level over days; burn-up at project level over stages
C.why: A burn-down is often used at team level over the days of an iteration; a burn-up at project or product level over stages or iterations (12.4.3).

whyNot.0: This reverses the usual levels of the two charts.
whyNot.1: The burn-up is usually a project or product level chart, not a team one.
whyNot.2: Burn-downs are usually team charts, not board charts.

C.q: The progress practice in PRINCE2 Agile mixes time-based and event-based controls. What does it ultimately determine?
options: Whether and how the project should proceed
Which user stories enter the next iteration
How changes to the baseline are approved
Who is accountable for each product
C.why: 5.3.1.7: the progress practice addresses the ongoing achievability of plans and ultimately determines whether and how the project should proceed.

whyNot.1: Choosing stories for an iteration happens in iteration planning, part of the team planning workshop.
whyNot.2: Approving baseline changes belongs to the issues practice.
whyNot.3: Accountability for products is set by the organization practice.

reteach.title: A fixed-price, fixed-date dinner party
reteach.question: If the guests arrive at 8 and the budget is spent, what can still change?

blocks.body: You have a fixed budget and guests arrive at 8. Checking the clock against a tolerance is pointless: 8 is 8. What you watch is the menu. The main course is a Must; the starter is a Should; the fancy dessert is a Could. If cooking runs slow, the dessert goes, not the arrival time. PRINCE2 Agile progress works the same way: watch what is delivered.

blocks.text: Running late is not fixed by moving the time: the flex is in what is delivered.

explain.body: Progress: monitor and compare actual against planned, forecast objectives and viability, and control deviations causing an exception (12.1).

test.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. The purpose of the [?] practice includes providing a forecast for the project's objectives and continued viability.
options: plans
progress
business case
risk
test.why: Forecasting objectives and continued viability is part of the progress practice purpose (12.1).

whyNot.0: Plans defines the products and the means to deliver them.
whyNot.2: The business case judges desirability, viability and achievability, but forecasting against plan is progress.
whyNot.3: Risk identifies, assesses and controls uncertainties.

explain.h: Zero tolerance on time and cost
explain.body: Time and cost have zero tolerance on all levels of plan, so progress focuses on what is delivered (Table 3.1, 12.3.1).

test.q: Which aspect normally flexes when an agile team cannot finish everything in a timebox?
options: Time
Cost
Lower-priority scope
Minimum viable benefits
test.why: Scope is flexed for Should and Could haves; time and cost have zero tolerance (Table 3.1).

whyNot.0: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan.
whyNot.1: Cost has zero tolerance on all levels of plan.
whyNot.3: Benefits are fixed at minimum viability and only flex above it.

explain.body: Burn charts show work done and still to do. Burn-down: team, days. Burn-up: project or product, iterations or stages (12.4.3).

test.q: Which chart is often used at project or product level to forecast completion dates?
options: Cumulative flow diagram
Team skill matrix
Iteration burn-down
Burn-up chart
test.why: A burn-up is a run chart of completed work against a deadline, often at project or product level, to forecast completion dates (12.4.3).

whyNot.0: A cumulative flow diagram shows workflow states and is mostly a team-level tool.
whyNot.1: A team skill matrix maps skills and gaps, not delivery progress.
whyNot.2: An iteration burn-down is usually a team-level chart over days.

explain.body: Reporting is taken seriously but often happens through workshops and visuals such as burn charts and dashboards. The PM may join stand-ups with the team's agreement (12.2, Table 12.1).

test.q: A project manager wants to attend a delivery team's daily stand-up. What does PRINCE2 Agile say?
options: The PM may attend with the delivery team's agreement
The PM should chair it to collect checkpoint data
The PM must send project support in their place
The PM attends once a week in place of a report
test.why: Table 12.1: the project manager may attend daily stand-ups with the delivery team's agreement.

whyNot.1: The stand-up belongs to the team; the PM does not chair it.
whyNot.2: There is no rule that project support attends in the PM's place.
whyNot.3: There is no weekly attendance rule replacing reports; attendance needs the team's agreement.
